blocks.x: So you made some records, huh? Yeah, I made records with Rudy Blair and Baby Dodge and George Lewis. You known Joey's finished a good while? Oh yes, indeed. We were like a family. That's why I don't understand why he didn't call here to let me know his mother had passed. I know he came here. He said, I wasn't going to leave out of town until I come see you. He said, his mother, every time he got ready to go somewhere to see somebody, she'd make out she's sick. I said, no, George, she's old and she ain't been seeing you much. And I said, she just wants you around. He said, oh, she just be putting on for you. He said, I can't stay up under. I've got to get out and look for money. So I said, he said, well, she fell. He said, I just told her stay in bed. He said, I didn't get no doctor or nothing. I told her stay in the bed and I rubbed her and I'll give her some kind of medicine. He said, give her. I said, well, if I was on my feet, I'd go there and see about her. He said, she'd be all right if she'd be up the next day or so. That's right. That's what it is. And my mind belonged to them people. I said, I'm going to call. And I said, no, I'll wait. With Krishna Baby, I said, I'm going to call Derek and tell him with Krishna Baby. I said, no, he'll call me. And no later than die. I don't know. Did Babe work with him much? Oh yeah, they played music a lot. They used to play. For all them white people, all the U.S. engineers, Babe would get the jobs and George and him sign them up, you know, picnics, weddings, and any kind of party they'd give, they'd see Babe. Babe would get pajo too. The last one he had, he had pajo on him because George was out of town. And he got another fella. What is his name? Henry, ain't he? He lived around there with played with his daddy. John. John. What instrument did he play? John. John, he played a horn. John Cajmy. Yeah, well I know John Cajmy. He's a clarinet player.

Yeah. My baby used to get him jobs too. He's the one that had the young tuxedo draft. Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah, that's him. When I may see him Tuesday, he's supposed to have a little funeral. Hmm? He's supposed to have a funeral Tuesday. Yeah, why? Up at the merry-go-round, Eagle and Hickory, you know? Oh yeah, you go where up there? Oh, anywhere I go in. I follow my job. Anytime there's any kind of music I like to hear. In my children come to me, they got some white

people down there following. I said, well, they always follow the band. You see, I don't believe they're from here. They look too nice to be from here. I said, one of them spoke to me just as nice. I said, well, they get from here then. Y'all were down there by the field down the street.
Well. But back to your records, how many tunes did you sing for making records? How many hymns?

I don't know. I sang, uh, couldn't hear nobody pray and wade in the water. And, uh, I sang about five of them. I sang about five of my nephew. He sang, Harold Lewis. You know him? I never met him, but I heard him funny. He, uh, he was living in Wellington, Delaware. He had a music place out there. He can play and sing. I had a piano not too long ago. I had to move out there. It was too crowded. He used to get there and

play and clown on it. When you, uh, sang for those records, they had a whole band with you? Yeah. Mm-hmm. Well, did they ever do that in church? No. They would never have a band like that in church. No, indeed.

Well, what do they have in churches now? Now, at Reverend Simpson, they have a horn and a piano, two, uh, piano and organ. And at our church, they have an organ and a piano. That's all. They have a horn. Who is Reverend Simpson? Right up here on Liberty Street. Near First.
Near that barbershop? Near Joseph's barbershop? Yeah. At the trombone play that slide. You know

Joseph and them too, huh? Oh yeah. My husband used to play with them too. Kaja, who was a clarinet player. And, um, when my husband played with him, though, he had, uh, Leo, Leo Sanjay, his cousin. That was my husband's cousin. He played, um, uh, banjo in that thing.
Yeah. And that's with, uh, with which one of the Joseph's? The one got the barbershop, I think.
Your husband was playing bass. The other one was coming from away. He got killed. He was living

away and he coming and got killed. Yeah, that's kind of. Got killed. Yeah. Nelson had the barbershop and he also had a brother work there who played bass. So it couldn't have been him. It couldn't be John. John is still alive. He's still cutting hair and playing bass. And I don't think he knows how old he is. He's way up in his ain't he? He's a old man. My husband was a little too old. When I and him got married,

he's, he's age 49, but I know different. He looked good at that time for his age, but I know different. What year did you get married? We married in, I can't remember. He was 31 or something like that.
You were married a long time ago. We were 31. And he said his age was 49.
Yeah. We often laughed about that afterwards. He'd never tell his right age. You know, on those
page? No. Mm-mm. You told him, say, come on now, babe, tell him your right age or something like that.

Mm-mm. He never would. He never would. And I laughed. I said, you know something? I said, I'm going to have more trouble. Sure enough, when he died, I did have trouble. Get somebody to prove his right age. Now, right now, it's the, his social security. I can't get it. I'm trying to get his right age. I done sent to, uh, they sent to the ain't in Washington no more. It's in Philadelphia. And that's where I had to send. And that gave his right age. They haven't sent it back to me yet, but Mr. Bartlow, Mr. Bartlow's brother out in St. John, sent me the correct age. And when he was born. Well, the church would show that out there. Yeah. The Catholic church where he was christened.
They keep brackets, you know. Mm-hmm.

So, uh, I don't know. He, never did get down. He just was fine, kept going and going. And the last week when he got in that bed, I knew that was all. He'd set up here before he'd get in the bed. So, why don't you lay down? You feel bad? I'll tell him to that. No, I'm feeling all right. We won't go and be fixing this shit. And be so weak. I could see the weakness in him. I said, babe, go lay down. I don't want to lay down. If I had a little drink of wine. So, I'd send one of them, I'd say, go get him a half a pint of wine. And I'd put it on ice. He said, ooh, that was good. I'd get out of here and walk to that corner of that and stand up a while and come back, sit right in the chair. I'm down and sit up there in a chair and everybody be sleeping. I'd hear him snowing. I said, why don't you get up and go to bed? I'm going. I'm sitting up here thinking. He was only in the bed a week when he died. He got so thin. I said to the doctor that had some doctors used to come in to see me about my legs and they used to give me the exercise in the bed, you know, pull them and pull my arms and just turn me every kind of way by the inside out. And I said, I believe my husband got T.Vs. So, one of them looked down and good examined him first and he got no T.Vs. So, he said, I'll tell you what you do. He said, you make him go down in there and take a test. For sure enough, he did. The children carried him down there. And they sent his back and said, he was negative, no T.Vs. But he had the ferocious of the livers. The thicker had cooked his livers. You know, that's what was there. No T.Vs whatsoever. I was glad of that. That's what she said.
So, he had such an age. I don't want to get you drunk and everything.
Yeah, he drank hard. Oh, he'd slip out and drink. We couldn't stop him. He'd slip out and get it. So, he was just one of those things.
I don't think you're right. Did you ever know George McCullough?

Yes, indeed. He died. Yes, indeed, I know George. George used to play with my husband. You see, George Howard. Howard been sick. I don't know if he will. He's got that liver too. Yeah, he was sick and kind of losing his mind when my husband died. He came up here.
Get back from that curb.
Oh. Get back to y'all. This young fella used to play a, oh, what is that name? We used to call him a nickname. Used to play banjo. Had to be here.
Oh, I know who you're talking about. He died too?

Yeah. Lawrence. Lawrence. Lawrence and Howard. George McCullough, George Lewis, my husband. And the fella used to play the drums. That little fella named Happy. Well. And then they had another one. He lived up here on Hall Street somewhere. Now he's a drunker. He used to play with them when he couldn't get happy. They would be leaving on a Saturday evening like this to go way down in Bali to play for the white folks. Well, they'd come over there and they'd start to drink. I'd be, have the fried pork chop and make sanders and everything for them. They'd drink back before they leave. Well, they wouldn't come back to a Sunday morning and play Saturday night and dance on Sunday, you know. Start Sunday evening playing over there. Well, they'd stay over there overnight. And they'd come back Monday morning. They did that for a long time.
They'd stay over there. They'd stay over there.
And the doctor had told George McCullough not to drink what he would drink. That killed him too.
Who played banjo on the record you made? Do you remember that?
I don't think we had a banjo player. We had George, Baby Dodge.
I don't think we used my husband on him.
Just George and Baby Dodge. Jerry. Jerry. When we made them records, did they have a banjo player here? Yes. Who? What? It was Lawrence, I believe. It was Lawrence. Yes, Lawrence.
How you feeling, Chad?
All right, Chad. How you?
Oh, I'm tired.
Yes, huh?
Yeah, I still am.
Now.
You know how you're working with a sucker?
Yes, indeed. Well, Lawrence was on it. Lawrence, Baby Dodge, George, and myself.
Did I tell you that he was in town?
Who?
Kid Punch, the trumpet player.
Punch, yeah? Mm-hmm.
He lives up in Carlton and simple and very dead, you know?
Mm-hmm. Oh, I ain't seen Punch in years and years and years. Yeah.
Well, he's a, he had a called black operation. Hmm.
All of them come down to something. I don't know.
I know your husband talked about Punch on the table.
Yeah. Oh, yeah. He, uh, Punch married, uh, somebody I know well, very well. But they separated and he left. Mm-hmm.
How you feel? Mm-hmm. I don't know.

I don't see nobody. I don't get out from the movie. Yeah. When I used to get out, I'd make all them fumes. Just like you do. I'd like little Louie on the fumes. I don't let it be music. They got to be feeling Carlton today. Reverend Scott.
Oh, yeah. I don't know.
Huh?
They're bearing him by committee.
Oh, no music.
No music. Yeah.
Because he belongs to young and true friends. And they do have music. I was wondering, was he going to have music?
No, I talked to Red Cross and he said he's bearing him by committee.
Mm-hmm.
Because, uh, I never did understand that by committee, how that works. They don't march at all.
No, 12 go out in the limousine. Mm-hmm.
There's 12 members, the president, the vice president, the secretary, we call the secretary, and the six committees of the club. That's what makes up the committees.
Do you belong to any of the authorities?
Yes, I do. I belong to one of the oldest colored clubs here, that's the Lady Tulane. Social Aid and Pledge Club down on Grabier near Roma.
I know that.

I belong to, I've been in that when it wasn't but a nickel of joy built up. I belong to the Lady Olympians, and I belong to the Golden Rule, and I belong to the Lady Dallashays, and I belong to the St. Stephen Benevolent. Then I am Estor. Eastern Estor? Yes. You remember my wife, you said.
Mm-hmm.

I was in more than that, but after I got sick and couldn't get around to do no work, well, I had to let some of them go. Looks like they'll take care of you. Well, to a certain extent, they'll give you, but they'll give you so much in a year and then no more. Oh. You see? They'll pay you three hours a week. After you get five weeks, you automatically drop them. Some of them give you a dollar and a half a week until death. I said, you got to have a doctor and send in a certificate every week. Well, a dollar and a half wouldn't pay you to send them a certificate. Yeah.
Unless you knew a doctor might well.
Hmm?
Unless you knew a doctor might well.

And I don't care how much you know them yet. They just want that almighty dollar. Mm-hmm. They don't do nothing but nothing. And they fill your blanks. That's 50 cents each time. Mm-hmm. Pretty good, Jackie. Very good.
You only make a dollar out of a deal then. Sure.

Since I was lost to the Good Citizen Insurance. I had to sell that back the other day. I'm waiting. The man might come Monday night and tell me what's what. And I was lost to that. I've been in there many years. I had to sell that back. So I couldn't keep them. And Babe was on the welfare when he died. But I wasn't on. So automatically I can't get on until I get myself straightened up with the age. You know. And his check come from the governor. Two days after he's dead I had to send it back. The U.S. engineers. I couldn't keep it. I had to send it back. So they don't give me nothing. See that just was security for him until death.
I didn't leave anything. And you never had social security yourself? No.

But now the lady told my daughter. See they've been running down there trying to tend to it for me. That if they get him on full night and back I'll get social security too. They got to have his agent. Have to have it in statement correct. Josh. They are right.
Handed.
Correct that he was. You know. Handed.

oh yeah you used to go uh over the river there at a nine miles point they used to call it on uh picnic uh like monday coming up that's a big picnic thing labor day fourth of july then the different clubs would have their annual picnic just like the two lane the two lane went last saturday on a big picnic it was last saturday they went to slide there now they got one coming up olympia they gonna have a picnic i don't know it's in this month but i don't know exactly the date because i don't go on none of them

well a picnic you go out of town or go somewhere off but a fish fry they have like here now they got one and later just was telling out that she's been waking all day they're gonna have a fish friday night chicken and fish and beer and all that selling that's jerry where tany i hear a crying blood back there she uh she they got one but that's for their church you see my church her church second baptist church all them churches gonna be towed out ain't gonna be down there no more so all of them is trying to get money together to build somewhere else they don't know where

oh they're gonna pay for them yeah they're gonna pay for them so they got to pay for them but they ain't gonna get it what they and just like our church our church is a beautiful church air condition and everything but we'll never get the money from the city what we done put out on that church they'll never give you that money all the new addition and all that's put onto that church we'll never get that back

well they used to have a man play a guitar you know some people had pianos in their house had piano music and some had guitars there a fellow with a guitar coming there he'd stay all night for a little or nothing drinking and eating and give him two dollars or so that'd be all he wanted play till broad daylight well the law wasn't strict then about what you do in your house that show you didn't break the law fighting you know you know

but you can't do that now because people come to your house drunk and cut up. You have to call the law for them. So I don't bother giving nothing like that. I didn't before I got crippled. I'd rather go out and work. I worked at the Undertaker because the people had got too funny.
You worked at an Undertaker?
Oh yeah, I used to work here at Majestic before I got out.
What did you do then?
Nightmade. I worked at Ms. Gertrude Gertrude Willis.
And you took care of that? What kind of job did you do last?

Nightmade too. Somebody die and make the car and soothe people. Put out the cups and saucers. If they didn't have a committee, well I'd serve them. If they have a committee, I'd just put the dishes out and when they'd finish, I'd see that everything was put back in the kitchen clean. That Barry Professor yesterday, I believe, old professor. I saw his picture in the paper. Yeah, well, he used to stay up there with me at night until I'd finish and walk me home here.
Well, he was a big man in the theater business.

Yeah. He was just like you see me. He wouldn't fix himself up or nothing. That old man had a head on him. He used to work with the papers too. Had a paper I used to call Brotherhood Eye to say he put that paper out. I don't know if he did or if he didn't. But anytime your record was bad, you went somewhere and you wanted to be somebody and you wasn't, he would show Prince your name in that paper. But they couldn't prove he was Prince. 된된 Did I ever ask you what year you came to the city? No, you didn't. And if you did, I couldn't tell you because I can't remember. I came here quite young. I don't remember the year, but I left out of Natchez College and came here because my dad died and I couldn't, I hadn't been there a whole trimester before I was out. I just left from high school and got in and had to come out because he died.
So you would come at your age when you came here?
Yeah.
How would you want?
How you sell the peaches?
Oh, I got big peaches. They're ten cents.
Give me five of them.
You ought to see them. You ought to see them, huh?
I don't know. I don't like all that. I never hit him.
You cannot get him down on the table. So you were starting Natchez College. Well, how old were you when you graduated from high school?
I don't know. I was too old. They say we were smart.
How old were you when the big storm came here? You remember the big storm?
In Natchez?
No, here.
The tornado you mean?
Yeah. The September storm.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I said call you. He gave me a peaches. Tip to him. Don't say nothing. Tell him don't say nothing. Don't talk to him.
I went here. Tell him to your mom. And I wait for you. Wait a minute, I'll turn this off. Mom, do you want to do peaches?
No. Me and the oprah? No.
We got oprah back there.
What I got from you.
Sweet potatoes, orange potatoes. That's all? Yeah. How much are these peaches?
Huh? Peaches is 10 as a piece. Alright. That's 50 cents.
Alright.
About 50 cents. About 50 cents.
About 50 cents.
We got okra back there what I got from you know. Sweet potatoes, orange potatoes. That's all. Yeah. How much do you eat peaches? Huh? Peaches is 10 as a piece. Alright. That's 50 cents. Alright.
I'm sorry to give me six. So the September storm in 1950, were you here for that storm?

Yeah. I had to come on here. My daddy died and my mother was here. They had separated. And I had to come on here. I couldn't stay out there in school. I had no money. And she got me a job right away working for Reverend on 4th Street where that steeple of the church went so many feet in the ground. I was working for that pastor at the time and his family. They lived right next door.
The steeple fell off and stuck in the ground.

Mm-hmm. Oh, people from 4th and near come to see that. It just blowed off and just struck down in the ground right in front of the church. And I had just got out the house to go run over to the grocery get some butter and bread so they'd have it in there that night. Because the storm was growing worse and the slates were just blowing off the house. And I had passed the thing when it happened. And she thought I had got caught there. And she fainted. And I was over at the grocery.
Well, how long had you been in town when that storm happened?
I hadn't been here long. I hadn't been here long. Two years or five years or one year? No, I hadn't been here five years. I hadn't been here five years. I'd been here about a year and a half then.
So you probably came in 1914 or so around in the morning. I had been here just about a year and a half. I was thinking that out pretty good.

Because my sister, she was small too. And my mother had them working for a man to market. He used to have to carry the people's market and the great big best. He'd put the names on them, the address. And they didn't have all these delivery trucks like they got. Now that was magazine market. A big market magazine in St. Mary's. Well, they used to go and get that market and soon the morning and deliver it around for him. He'd pay them what he wants and they'd give them lights and deliver them. The people didn't buy them things. They had lights. They'd give you that to make a big pot. Give them the peas feed and the hog hedge. My mom used to make hog hedge keys out of that. He'd just give it to us because they'd wait for him. You know, can't stuff around. And he didn't pay them a salary. Like, you know, he'd give them a dollar or two dollars. But he'd give them plenty of meat. And other butchers would say, well, you go in the same address. This is something. Give them a so-and-so. Well, they'd give them chop or so. They always had plenty of fresh meat.
Do you remember Henry's, you know, his funeral? His who? His funeral. Oh, yeah. I was in that funeral.

They say that was one of the, uh, places the city ever had. That's right. You know it was large. You know where the St. Mary's Cemetery is. I can't place that now. I suspect Hickory. Hickory and Lowell Eye. I know where that is. Well, one part of the people was getting out there and the other part was still getting in at the house. And the house was at, um, Hickory and Hickory. Right on the corner. The corner house was at Hickory.
Is it Cross-Carrot? I mean, uh, St. Charles. Cross St. Charles. I know exactly where Hickory is. Uh-huh. Yeah, I've been up in that neighborhood. There's plenty of-
Well, they had, uh, two bands. Two bands or three bands. Anyhow, I believe Happy was toting his drum. They had it all draped with crepe. We wasn't playing it at all.
Which Happy was that? Little Happy. The one that's alive now? Uh-huh. He was on the taxi call. Plays with the Eureka bands. Yeah, I don't know where Happy lived, but I knew it was him.

Not red Happy? Uh-uh. Not red. A dark one. Yeah, there's two of the Happys that always get to- No, I don't mean red. I mean the dark one. So Happy carried him as he knows? Uh-huh. Well, I'll be. That must have been a big one. It was a funeral, I'm telling you. Everybody talked about that funeral. How many bands did that have? I think they had two or three if I'm mistaken. Because it happened so quick. I just left the boy the day before. He played a funeral out, St. Mary, and Chippewa. And he said, we got another one to play tomorrow. He said, in Carlton. I said, yeah. He said, don't you come and bring that child. He said, that's too much of walking. I said, I'll be there. I used to follow the band everywhere they went. So, uh, I went on home and I was washing. After he knocked off, he come by there and they bought me some beer and we talked. He said, I see you tomorrow. And I said, yeah. He said, don't bring the baby. I said, uh-uh. Me and her like to dance. That was my little niece I had. A little bit of thing like that and come in here just now. So we was home there the next morning. I said, well, let me hurry up. I said, because that funeral of them called them for one o'clock. I don't wash them so well. Well, I just remember who it was coming there and say, is your name this place? I said, yeah. I said, I want to take the corner grocery on the phone. I went to the corner and I answered. And his sister said to me, say, Bernice? I said, yeah. I said, Henry just died. I said, what Henry? I thought you were going to tell me my uncle had died. His daddy, you know.
She said, little Henry. I said, what? She said, he just died there.

Well, I got back there one night. It was a client in Magnolia. They had this little place, restaurant. I got back there. I seen so many people. I seen the police. I said, my God, it's true. So I went on up in there and he was looking. Couldn't get him to the hospital because he died right there. I said, somebody had given him some poison whiskey. I don't know what to say. The woman, what he had, had given it to him. He was going to marry. Well, he had been punished the house out for the girl. He had done what? Punished the house for a young girl and had everything in it. He was going to leave out the house with this woman and marry her. He wasn't married to that woman. They just came with her. And they said something the fellow in the band told him.
We never did find out who did it though. Well, times were really bad then about that.
Yeah. Everybody was upset. He died down like anything else.
Get paralyzed. Do you remember Robert Taylor, the trumpet play? He was supposed to get paralyzed. Yes, indeed. Yes, indeed. I know Robert. He kicked a woman down. She was supposed to fix him.

Yeah, they say that. They say that child. That's what Punch told me. People used to be bad doing things, but I can't get these children to believe nothing like that. That was true.
